name: Saw palmetto
lead: Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) is a small palm native to the subtropical southeastern United States and Mexico. Extracts of its berries are sold as supplements for prostate symptoms and, increasingly, for hair loss [1][2]. It is among the botanical products promoted as natural DHT blockers because extracts have antiandrogenic properties in laboratory studies [3][4].

The hair-loss rationale people cite is a chain: androgenetic alopecia is driven by dihydrotestosterone (DHT), formed from testosterone by the enzyme 5-alpha-reductase; saw palmetto extracts are described as inhibiting that enzyme, so users take them hoping to slow miniaturization and keep more hair, either on their own or alongside minoxidil or finasteride [3][4][4]. Herbal alternatives are frequently discussed because people want options with fewer of the side effects reported for conventional drugs [4].

Published reviews of saw palmetto in hair loss describe a small number of trials. A 2020 systematic review identified five randomised trials and two cohort studies reporting positive effects of oral and topical saw palmetto-containing supplements in androgenetic alopecia and telogen effluvium, while noting that robust high-quality data are lacking [3]. More recent industry-linked randomised trials of proprietary extracts in self-perceived thinning hair have been published [5][6][7].

For prostate symptoms, Wikipedia reports that as of 2023 there is no scientific evidence that the extract is effective for benign prostatic hyperplasia or cancer, though an earlier review of one standardised extract found it may relieve urinary symptoms [1]. Reviews of herb-drug interactions place saw palmetto among supplements with a low likelihood of drug interactions [8], and a bleeding review did not associate it with bleeding [9].
infobox: Well tolerated; mild, infrequent side effects [22]

paras: Saw palmetto is taken orally or applied topically in products for male and female pattern hair loss and self-perceived thinning. Reviews of natural products for androgenetic alopecia include saw palmetto among candidates, alongside caffeine, melatonin, rosemary oil and pumpkin seed oil, based on small clinical studies [10][11].

Hair-loss communities discuss saw palmetto as a natural alternative or add-on to finasteride and minoxidil. A reviewer of herbal options groups it with other plant extracts that act on 5-alpha-reductase and describes interest as driven by drawbacks of conventional drugs such as sexual side effects and scalp irritation [4]. Some forum posters say they took large amounts of extract to lower DHT [23].

The extract is widely used for lower urinary tract symptoms from benign prostatic hyperplasia. Reviews list it among herbal drugs used for that condition [12]. Trials include a US phase 3 study and several others registered on ClinicalTrials.gov [13][14][15].

Hair: the 2020 systematic review summarised effects such as a 60 percent improvement in overall hair quality, a 27 percent improvement in total hair count, increased density in 83.3 percent of patients and stabilised progression in 52 percent across various saw palmetto-containing supplements, with no serious adverse events, while calling for larger trials [3]. These products often contained other ingredients.

A 2023 double-blind placebo-controlled study randomised 80 men and women aged 18 to 50 with mild-to-moderate androgenetic alopecia to a standardised saw palmetto oil (2 to 3 percent beta-sitosterol) in oral or topical forms, or placebo, over 16 weeks, and reported reduced hair fall and improved growth [5]. Two further randomised trials of proprietary extracts in adults with self-perceived thinning hair reported 90-day and 180-day results [6][7]. These studies were of branded ingredients and the abstracts available here do not give effect sizes.
A systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia has also been published [16].

A 2025 randomized trial reported 90-day results of a proprietary bioactive fatty acids extract in adults with self-perceived thinning hair, and a 2026 trial reported 180-day results of a novel extract [6][7]. A systematic review and network meta-analysis of dietary supplements in androgenetic alopecia has been published [11][16]. NIH's National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health says a few small studies tested oral and topical use for male pattern hair loss and that the evidence is too limited to draw conclusions [22].
Prostate: a 2000 randomised trial and literature search, a 2024 uroflowmetry trial and the CAMUS and PERLES studies examined saw palmetto and related extracts for urinary symptoms [14][15][17][18].

For urinary symptoms, the NIH summary says a 2023 review of 27 studies found little or no benefit when the herb was used alone, and that two NIH-funded trials of saw palmetto alone, one at up to three times the usual dose, found no improvement in benign prostatic hyperplasia symptoms; it concludes saw palmetto is probably not helpful for BPH urinary symptoms [22]. A 2016 review of the standardised extract Permixon described it as safe and possibly helpful for urinary symptoms [1]. The CAMUS trial enrolled 369 participants and the PERLES study 833 [17][18]. A 1998 JAMA systematic review and a 2006 New England Journal of Medicine paper on saw palmetto for BPH are among the most cited studies [24][25].

Trials in alopecia reported good tolerability [3]. A review of herbal supplement-drug interactions classed saw palmetto with those having low likelihood of interactions with most medications [8]. A bleeding review found no association with bleeding [9]. A 1999 laboratory study examined inhibition of human sperm motility by several herbs, including saw palmetto [19].

NIH describes the herb as well tolerated in research lasting up to three years, with mild and infrequent side effects that may include digestive symptoms, dizziness and headache; it does not appear to affect PSA readings, and it may be unsafe during pregnancy or breastfeeding [22]. NIH advises people taking medicines to consult a health care provider before using any herbal product [22]. In a hair loss forum thread, one poster who had taken a lot of saw palmetto years earlier to lower DHT wondered whether it was connected to symptoms they were now experiencing [23]; no study has established such a link.

Extracts contain fatty acids and phytosterols and are described as inhibiting 5-alpha-reductase and possibly androgen receptor binding; reviews attribute these antiandrogenic properties as the rationale for hair and prostate use [3][4][12].

Laboratory work and reviews describe lipidosterolic extracts with antiandrogenic activity; reviews of herbal alternatives place saw palmetto among plant extracts proposed to inhibit 5-alpha-reductase and reduce DHT-driven miniaturization, a mechanism that is also the target of finasteride [4][3]. Human trials have mostly measured hair counts, density or self-rated hair quality rather than scalp DHT levels.
Indigenous peoples of the southeastern US used the fruit and fibres, and the fruit was historically a food [1]. Saw palmetto was discussed in a medical journal as early as 1912 [20].

Saw palmetto (Serenoa repens) is the only species in its genus, a slow-growing fan palm 2-3 m tall that can live 500-700 years in some Florida populations [1]. Native peoples used the leaves for thatching and the fruit may have been used by the Seminoles and Lucayans against fish poisoning; fibres have been found as far north as Wisconsin and New York, suggesting wide trade [1].

lore.intro: Saw palmetto appears in hair-loss discussions as the most-cited natural DHT blocker, usually weighed against finasteride [4][23].

claims.claim: Saw palmetto blocks DHT and can slow hair loss
claims.believers: Posters say plant extracts inhibit 5-alpha-reductase and describe taking it instead of or alongside finasteride and minoxidil [23].
claims.experts: A 2020 systematic review found five randomized trials and two cohort studies reporting positive effects of saw palmetto-containing supplements but noted robust high-quality data are lacking; NIH says evidence is too limited for conclusions [3][22].

claims.claim: Higher-dose or standardized extracts work better for hair
claims.believers: Some forum users take large amounts hoping for a stronger DHT effect [23].
claims.experts: A 2023 trial used a standardised saw palmetto oil (2 to 3 percent beta-sitosterol) in oral and topical forms for 16 weeks [5]. No trial has established that more extract means more hair.

claims.claim: Saw palmetto is a gentler option than prescription DHT blockers
claims.believers: Hair-loss communities cite fewer side effects as the reason for choosing herbal options [4].
claims.experts: Trials in alopecia reported good tolerability, and NIH describes side effects as mild and infrequent [3][22]. Direct head-to-head trials against finasteride are not among the studies reviewed here.

angle.text: People take oral saw palmetto capsules or use topical oils as a plant-based DHT blocker for male and female pattern hair loss. Small trials of saw palmetto-containing products report improvements in hair counts and quality.
